insufficiencies.note: The base lexical extract supplies rich biographical entries for the four Babylonian names given at 1:7 (Belteshazzar, Shadrach, Meshach, Abednego) and for Ashpenaz/Melzar, but no etymological gloss for what any of these NAMES themselves mean -- only bare transliteration. Babylonian court renamings of this kind often carry theophoric elements (invoking a Babylonian deity), which would bear directly on this passage's own theme of allegiance/devotion (already registered at Nebuchadnezzar/1:2's dedication of the temple vessels to his own god) -- but this cannot be verified or analyzed from the data actually available, so it is named here rather than supplied from remembered/external knowledge.

Already flagged at operation.set as retain_referential (Daniel/1:17/ordinal 1) rather than resolved there -- carried forward here as a live interpretive fork, to be weighed against how the same construction behaves elsewhere in the corpus as more chapters accumulate, not settled in the abstract now.

emergent_questions.question_text: A repeated structural pattern runs across this whole passage -- resolve (1:8) -> risk/proposal (1:11-13) -> observable proof (1:14-16, largely silent) -> recognition (1:17->1:19-20) -- recurring at both Daniel's own individual scale (1:8-13) and the four-member group's shared scale (1:14-20). This is a genuine literary/structural observation about the chapter's own composition, not itself a phenomenon of any single HIB (kept out of the phenomena register per phenomenon.set/not-literary-pattern) -- logged here instead.

quality_checks.emergent-question-not-resolvable-now: A whole-passage compositional pattern by definition can't be resolved within any single verse/HIB phenomenon entry -- that is exactly why phenomenon.set/not-literary-pattern excludes it from the phenomena register.

emergent_questions.question_text: Nebuchadnezzar's own act of religious devotion (crediting his god with the victory, 1:2) is not followed up on anywhere else in this chapter. Does this set up the book's larger, later theme (explicit in Dan 2-4) of Nebuchadnezzar's own gradual movement toward recognizing the true God? A genuine cross-chapter interpretive question, not resolvable from Dan 1 alone.
